section_summary: This section completes a 1934 consular report on Japanese immigration, commerce, agricultural landholding, and press criticism in Peru, then presents diplomatic despatches from 1934–1936 concerning Japanese economic penetration and alleged strategic ambitions. The documents range from alarmist anonymous letters and hostile newspaper campaigns to F. E. Bresee’s comparatively reassuring investigation of the Japanese community around Chimbote. The final pages begin an enclosed 1935 Spanish-language study of international quota systems, the world economic crisis, Japanese commercial expansion, and protection of Peru’s textile industry.

subfiles.title: Notes on Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.about: A wide-ranging report assesses Japanese immigration, commercial activity, agricultural landholding, alleged military preparation, and hostile press reaction in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion begins with Pinto Basurco’s geopolitical speculation about Japanese ambitions in South America and rumors of militarily trained Japanese residents. It then reviews immigration statistics, Japanese participation in retailing and manufacturing, and the growing leasing of agricultural land in coastal valleys. The report emphasizes Peruvian landowners’ and farmers’ alarm, reproduces C. A. Lummis’s proposed restrictions on Japanese tenants and labor, and notes Japanese-language newspapers published in Lima.

subfiles.title: La agricultura nacional
subfiles.about: Lummis warns that Japanese tenants are gaining control of Peruvian coastal farmland and proposes statutory preferences for Peruvian farmers and laborers.
subfiles.summary: Spanish clipping argues Japanese agricultural settlement raises economic and racial dangers for Peru; Lummis recommends reserving eighty percent of tenanted land and jobs for Peruvians.

subfiles.title: Document File Note 723.942/15
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references Dearing’s despatch reporting Peruvian plans to halt Japanese economic penetration.
subfiles.summary: File note 723.942/15: Peru's foreign minister said the government would act against Japanese economic penetration (despatch of November 3, 1934).

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3670: Japanese Economic Penetration in Peru
subfiles.about: Dearing reports the Peruvian foreign minister’s determination to curb Japanese economic penetration and colonization.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 3670: Peru's foreign minister links denouncing the 1924 treaty and irrigated-land limits to stopping Japanese accumulation, citing California's experience and worry about Japanese colonization in the Montana, Brazil and Putumayo.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4007: Enclosing Further Information Regarding Japanese Influence
subfiles.about: Dearing transmits an anonymous Peruvian letter alleging expansive Japanese military and racial ambitions.
subfiles.summary: Dearing characterizes the enclosure as absurd but potentially indicative of attitudes toward Japan in Peru and elsewhere. He notes an estimated 26,000 Japanese residents in Peru, Japan’s successful commercial penetration, and South America’s importance as a possible source of raw materials.

subfiles.title: Anonymous Peruvian Letter on Alleged Japanese Aims
subfiles.to: Secretary of the American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: An anonymous writer repeats a Japanese acquaintance’s purported claims about conquest, racial war, and Japanese settlement in the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Anonymous letter claims a former Japanese soldier described plans to divide China, defeat the US, seize California and settle the Americas, with Japanese immigrants in Peru and Brazil as waiting soldiers.

subfiles.title: Translation of Anonymous Peruvian Letter on Alleged Japanese Aims
subfiles.to: Secretary of the American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: This English translation renders the anonymous Spanish letter alleging Japanese plans for conquest in Asia and the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Translation of the anonymous letter: a former Japanese soldier's program to divide China, defeat the US, take California and dominate whites, with migrants as methodically placed military men.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4065: Japanese Activities Near Chimbote, Peru
subfiles.about: Dearing forwards an Adventist mission leader’s investigation of frequently exaggerated rumors about Japanese activities near Chimbote.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 4065: Dearing asks Adventist mission president Bresee to investigate Chimbote; the largely negative findings are valuable and may be shared with the Navy.

subfiles.title: Confidential Report: Japanese Activities in and around Chimbote, Peru
subfiles.about: Bresee surveys Japanese occupations, property, imports, immigration, population, and attitudes in the Chimbote area.
subfiles.summary: Bresee finds about 150 Japanese in Chimbote in restaurants, barber shops and small stores, owning about 125,000 soles of property, with little immigration and no overt hostility.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Anti-Japanese Feeling in Peru
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Lima report on renewed anti-Japanese sentiment and recommends it to trade officials.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern memo: anti-Japanese feeling in Peru has revived through press attacks, legislation, trade restrictions and merchant protests; the embassy report convincingly shows Peruvian alarm.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4371: Letter Concerning Danger from the Japanese
subfiles.from: R. M. de Lambert, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards J. Vercellone’s appeal for immediate United States action against an alleged Japanese menace.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 4371 transmits Vercellone's letter on the Japanese danger; staff compare it with a June 18, 1935 anonymous letter and think the same person wrote both.

subfiles.title: A Norte America
subfiles.to: North America and the United States
subfiles.about: Vercellone urges white unity and a preemptive American response to imagined Japanese plans for Asian conquest of the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Spanish letter urges preventing European war so white nations can unite against Japan, claiming Japan deceptively controls China and might attack with huge numbers of cheap aircraft.

subfiles.title: Translation: To North America
subfiles.to: North America and the United States
subfiles.about: This English translation presents Vercellone’s warning about alleged Japanese domination of China and plans against the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Translation of 'To North America': urges white unity against Japan, claims bamboo aircraft and fuel on Japanese islands, and asks the US to settle Europe's disputes and destroy Japanese ambitions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4460: Anti-Japanese Sentiment in Peru Increases
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The embassy documents a renewed Peruvian campaign against Japanese immigration, capital, trade practices, and textile imports.
subfiles.summary: The despatch surveys hostile coverage in Lima newspapers, disputes over compliance with employment laws, and textile quotas adopted after denunciation of the commercial treaty with Japan. It recounts Japanese merchant protests, Peruvian allegations of unfair competition, debate over a Japanese-backed omnibus line, controversy over Japanese land claims and control of the Churín baths, and calls to restrict Japanese capital and immigration. It also reports the creation of a Japanese merchants’ association, visits by Japanese commercial representatives, and defenses of Japanese immigration by Francisco Gómez de la Torre and Pedro E. Paulet.

subfiles.title: El Sistema de Contingentes en el Comercio Internacional
subfiles.about: The pamphlet examines international quota systems, Japanese commercial expansion, most-favored-nation rules, and the protection of Peruvian industry.
subfiles.summary: The title pages, preface, and contents outline sections on the postwar world economy, Japanese commercial expansion, import and export quotas, the most-favored-nation clause, and Peru’s cotton-textile industry. The surviving text discusses the political and social crisis after the First World War, periodic economic crises, protectionism, monetary disorganization, and the Great Depression. Statistical tables compare securities, wholesale prices, industrial production, Latin American debt, and countries’ abandonment of the gold standard before the text turns to competing monetary policies associated with the United States, Britain, and France.
